A potential approach to speed up the builds of mul- tiple configurations is to do incremental build, i.e., to not clean the build environment and reuse previous builds when building a new configuration. Previous exploratory studies showed some benefits and limitations of incre- mental build, but mainly on small configurable software systems and on a limited set of close configurations. However, for large configuration spaces, little is known whether the large distance across configurations impacts the correctness and efficiency of incremental build. This paper presents PyroBuildS, a new approach to speed up incremental builds while keeping reproducibility, featuring a configuration variation oper- ator parameterized by two deny lists of problematic options and a mutation size (diversity). We evaluate PyroBuildS through an empirical study on three large com- plex configurable systems, namely Linux, BusyBox, and ToyBox, with re- spectively 18637, 1078, 330 configuration options. The design of PyroBuildS is directly informed by our empirical findings, which revealed specific configu- ration options and conditions under which incremental builds are ineffective or counterproductive. Second, we run an in-depth empirical study of in- cremental build on three large complex configurable systems, namely Linux, BusyBox, and Toybox, with respectively 18637, 1078, 330 configuration op- tions. We first observe that incrementally building the random configurations significantly reduces build time for BusyBox, and Toybox, with an average gain of 15% to 20%; incremental build thus pays off as such. However, we show that some options can be detrimental to build time; PyroBuildS is able to avoided them. For Linux, however, incremental build on random configurations just backfires, taking more time than with clean builds. When incrementally building mutated configurations, we observe a sys- tematic gain in execution time from 16% to 22%, and a diversity in terms of options that are changed between configurations. Build and Make A build system specifies how to translate source code into a deliverable. The developer typically declares: 1) rules on how to compile a source code, 2) which libraries to include, and 3) how to link them all together in order to obtain an executable. Make Feldman (1979b) is one of the most popular build systems Mcin- tosh et al. (2015). Build specifications are declared in Makefiles that are spread out in the subdirectories of a project. Makefiles contain 1) (leaf-) rules whose trigger is a filename to generate a library or object/executable file, with its "recipe" depending on source files 2) rules that trigger other rules. To build a project, Make starts by reading the Makefile at the root of the project, then recursively goes into subdirectories. On its way, Make builds a dependency graph of the relations between rules and spawns a build process to satisfy each rule. On its first invocation, Make checks that all rules are satisfied. If a target file does not exist, Make produces it according to the specification. Otherwise, it checks the timestamps of its dependencies: if the target file is older than one of its dependencies, it must be recompiled. This process is propagated on the whole rule dependency graph. For a first build of a project, Make does a full build because none of the target files exist yet. Importantly, a second invocation of Make does nothing if no mod- ification was done. Typically, a call to Make checks timestamps and triggers the rules impacted by the last file modification. If the specifications are cor- rectly written Bezemer et al. (2017), this process does not rebuild the whole project every time, thus saving resources. This process of rebuilding only the minimum necessary parts of the build is called an incremental build. It has been well-known and widely used for decades. 2.2. Challenges and Motivation A number of works and techniques exist to optimize the compilation (i.e., build) of systems after commits Cao et al. (2017b); Feldman (1979a); Tichy (1986); Schwanke and Kaiser (1988); Mitchell (2012); baz ([n.d.]); Erdweg et al. (2015); Konat et al. (2018); Hammer et al. (2015); Maudoux and Mens (2018). Building numerous varied configurations of large configurable sys- tems is an important but expensive task. However, a much lower number of works pertain to optimising (i.e., decreasing the cost of) massive builds of large configurations. The most commonly deployed solution is quite costly, since it just consists in applying successive, independent clean builds, not de- creasing resources’ usage at all and missing the opportunity to reuse already build artefacts. Incremental build with Make has the potential to speeding up build and saving resources. However, these benefits have only been shown on build after commits: changing a configuration and thus options’ values can lead to significant files’ differences. Furthermore, exploratory studies on configu- ration build on very small configurable systems with up to 40 configuration options, and showed mixed effective results Randrianaina et al. (2022b). Whether those benefits also occur on configuration build of large complex configurable systems with thousands of options thus remains largely unex- plored. To the best of our knowledge, no thorough investigation exists on the use of incremental build on large complex configurable systems. The next sections detail our approach and empirical study aiming at filling this gap. 3. The key idea behind PyroBuildS is to carefully control the variations ap- plied to the configurations being built to ensure reproducibility and reduce build time. We first develop a variation operator capable of mutating a given configuration based on three key parameters: a deny list of options that should not be changed, a deny list of options that should not be selected, and a change size that determines the number of options to change. This data-based approach serves two purposes: (1) understanding the specifics of each subject system (e.g., determining if randconfig poses problems for a given system); and (2) parameterizing the change magnitude and the deny lists for these systems. 3.1. PyroBuildS leverages the idea that “close” configurations can be built incrementally. In such cases, the build system reuses prior build artifacts thus saving time by not rebuilding everything from scratch. To select "close" configurations, PyroBuildS employs a vari- ation mechanism that mutates a given configuration repeatedly, creating a chain of local changes. After m such variations, the final configuration can differ substantially from the original base configuration because these small changes accumulate, akin to a spark traveling further and further from the rocket. This approach produces an interesting diversity of configurations while retaining the efficiency of incremental builds. While it would be possi- ble to generate each variation directly from the base configuration, chaining allows more distant configurations to emerge through incremental changes. In other words, the m-th variation can accumulate all prior modifications, ef- fectively reaching parts of the configuration space that a single-step mutation might not. Incremental Build vs. Clean Build. Once PyroBuildS finishes one lo- cal chain, it selects another base configuration (typically randomly sampled) 12 to explore a more distant region of the configuration space. When transi- tioning from one base to another, incremental builds might still reuse some artifacts, but if the two configurations are truly distant, the savings could be marginal. In these cases, PyroBuildS may resort to a clean rebuild. Thus, PyroBuildS always benefits from incremental build within a local chain of variations, and optionally uses it across base configurations when it remains cost-effective. Moreover, this covers the scenario of building specific config- urations required by developers (e.g., for a specific customer or hardware) that may not benefit from incremental build. Threats to validity We now discuss internal and external threats to validity Wohlin et al. (2012). Internal validity. We first measured the time performance of clean and incremental builds. The main risk lies in the interference of measurements with other running software. To counter this risk, we used a dedicated server where only our experiment was executed. We further isolated the build envi- ronment Docker image with only the required build tools and dependencies. We repeated the builds three times to reduce variability and ensure more reliable averages. As part of our experiments, a campaign of Linux builds took several days. The longer build times naturally mitigate minor fluctua- tions, reducing the need for multiple iterations. Additionally, as part of our exploratory experiments, we also observed consistent build times when re- peating, further supporting our approach. Overall, we are confident that our experimental data are reliable for Linux. We considered diversity by looking at the number of options that are activated during the build. Other metrics could also be considered, such as the impacted source code. However, the diff size of options is a good indicator for the diversity of a given configuration. External validity. We experimented on three systems (Toybox, Busy- box, Linux kernel) that are C-based, highly configurable software systems with the Make build system. Though variability-aware analysis is relevant in many engineer- ing contexts, our interest differs and consists in concretely building a sample of (possibly distant and diverse) configurations with an unexplored approach – incremental build. Al-Hajjaji et al. Al-Hajjaji et al. (2017, 2019) focused onoptimizingtheorderofatestedsetofconfigurations, byselectingthemost dissimilar configuration to the previous one to be built. However, while the authors incrementally select the configurations based on a similarity priori- tization criterion, they do not perform incremental build. Sampling configu- rations is subject to intensive research Alves Pereira et al. (2020); Jamshidi et al. (2018); Souto et al. (2017); Thüm et al. (2014); Heradio et al. (2022). However, incremental build brings new challenges. As empirically shown for Linux, incremental build is not effective when picking random configurations since the distance and differences across configurations are too important. In a sense, we develop in our work a new sampling procedure to either locally or globally explore configurations, avoiding the trap of changing values of problematic options. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to quan- tify and evaluate the use of incremental build on large configurable systems. We offer valuable learned lessons on when incremental build works and when not, especially in relation to the diff sizes of the configurations to be built incrementally. 8. Conclusion In this paper, we introduced PyroBuildS, an innovative approach to re- duce, through incremental builds, the computational cost of building large and complex configurable systems. Although incremental builds have been studied in the context of post-commit changes, their advantages in terms of configurations and large complex configuration spaces have not been fully understood. Our work and PyroBuildS address this gap. Our empirical evaluation on Linux, BusyBox, and ToyBox demonstrated that PyroBuildS effectively maintains build correctness while achieving sub- stantial reductions in build time. Gains with incremental build varied from 33 15% to 20% with random configurations and from 16% to 22% with mutated configurations. We identified specific problematic options that hinder in- cremental build effectiveness, allowing PyroBuildS to avoid these and ensure systematic gains. We have shown that "just" applying incremental builds can be counterproductive, and so that the three parameters of PyroBuildS that control configuration generation are crucial. Prior studies reported exploratory results on small configurable systems, with both negative and positive effects of incremental build. Our detailed analysis now explains these mixed outcomes, and PyroBuildS offers a way to improve the situation on large complex configurable systems. Our recommendations for using PyroBuildS are as follows. For BusyBox and ToyBox, PyroBuildS speeds up builds regardless of the distances across configurations. Hence, randconfig can be used out of the box. To explore more locally, a change size of 10 provides a good balance of diversity and speed-up, though this value can be increased if necessary. Overall, PyroBuildS is capable of achieving high diversity while speeding up builds by picking random configurations. For Linux, PyroBuildS relies on traditional, clean builds in the case of ran- dom configurations or pairs of configurations with large differences. These cases are straightforward to detect, enabling the avoidance of negative gains. We recommend relying on PyroBuildS to generate local variations of configu- rationswhereincrementalbuildspayoff. Thatis,PyroBuildScansignificantly reducebuildtimewhilestillprovidinggooddiversity,asitmodifiesmorethan 100 option values per local variation. A possible exploration strategy is to use random configurations as bases (with clean builds) and then incremen- tally build mutated configurations around them. PyroBuildS can effectively implement this process. Overall, we believe that PyroBuildS provides actionable insights and prac- tical support for developers, maintainers, and CI practitioners aiming to ac- celerate the build processes of highly configurable systems. While it is up to these stakeholders to define an appropriate exploration strategy—e.g., choosing between random or local configuration changes—PyroBuildS offers (1) a tool that facilitates controlled configuration generation and incremen- tal building, and (2) empirically grounded recommendations to avoid pitfalls and guide effective use of incremental builds. Infuturework,weaimtoapplyincrementalbuildsinotherscenarios,such as performance learning or testing patches in configurable systems, where 34 both code evolution and configuration changes must be managed. For in- stance, Yildiran et al. Yıldıran et al. (2024) addressed the challenge of deter- mining the optimal configurations to test patches in Linux project commits. Building on their approach, we plan to integrate PyroBuildS to assess its im- pact and potential benefits. This requires a specific effort to carefully avoid selecting configurations that are too distant or include problematic options. Moreover, PyroBuildS could also be integrated in a CI. Indeed, we can see PyroBuildS being integrated with KernelCI and Intel 0-day for example. For example, theideawouldbetobuilddefaultconfigurationsateachreleaseand turn around them in a firework analogy with incremental builds. This would strengthen the confidence in testing the default configurations as it is done by KernelCI and extend the number of tested random configurations by Intel 0-day with small extra resources. Finally, we plan to test PyroBuildS on con- figurable systems with a different build system and in different programming languages for more generalizable results. 9. JSON: Name: pyrobuilds_incremental_mutation Title: Controlled mutation and deny-list guided incremental builds to accelerate exploration of large configuration spaces while preserving build reproducibility Short Hypothesis: Applying a variation operator that mutates base configurations with a bounded mutation size and excludes options in reproducibility and performance deny lists yields incremental-build sequences whose mean build time is at least 15% lower than corresponding clean builds and produce bitwise-identical binaries for at least 99% of successful builds on target large configurable systems. Related Work: Existing approaches to reduce multi-configuration build cost fall into three categories: (1) classical incremental/heuristic build systems that optimize rebuilds after source changes but assume small, localized edits; (2) configuration sampling and variability-aware analyses that reduce the number of configurations to test but do not change the cost per build and often do not scale to very large configuration spaces; (3) ordering or scheduling techniques that attempt to find an optimal incremental build order for a given fixed set of configurations. Limitations of these approaches are: incremental build research assumes commit-sized edits and breaks down when many options differ; sampling methods either do not scale to thousands of options or cannot guarantee build-time savings; ordering techniques require the full target set a priori and do not handle dynamic on-the-fly exploration; and solver-based repair or synthesis tools struggle to scale or to preserve reproducible binary outputs. Prior work also lacks actionable methods to avoid options that systematically cause non-reproducible or costly incremental rebuilds. Abstract: Building and testing large configurable software systems is computationally expensive because many configuration variants must be compiled. Incremental builds can reuse prior artifacts to reduce cost, but they often fail when configurations differ widely or when specific options cause non-reproducible outputs or excessive recompilation. We propose a practical approach that couples a controlled configuration variation operator with two deny lists—one for options known to hinder reproducibility and one for options known to hinder incremental speedup—and a mutation-size parameter to bound differences between successive builds. The method generates chains of local mutations from multiple base configurations, performing incremental builds inside each chain and clean builds between distant bases. The primary contribution is an operational pipeline that (1) constrains exploration to configuration changes that preserve reproducibility and enable artifact reuse, (2) quantifies the tradeoff between diversity and build-time savings, and (3) provides an empirical protocol to discover problematic options for future runs. We expect this approach to substantially lower aggregate build time during large-scale configuration exploration while maintaining binary reproducibility for the vast majority of builds. Experiments: Datasets: Linux kernel (representative mainline version with ~18k Kconfig options), BusyBox (representative stable release ~1k options), Toybox (representative release ~300 options). For each system use the official Kconfig/Kbuild setup and randconfig/defconfig where needed. Baselines: (A) clean builds for each target configuration, (B) naive incremental builds using successive randconfig pairs (no deny lists, unconstrained mutation), (C) incremental builds ordered by an existing ordering technique (where feasible), and (D) incremental builds without the mutation-size bound but with deny lists. Method under test: PyroBuildS controlled mutation operator with reproducibility and performance deny lists and configurable mutation size. Experimental parameters: select n=100 base configurations per system, for each base generate m=10 variants using PyroBuildS (mutation sizes per system: Linux=1, BusyBox=10, Toybox=10) and m=10 random variants per base for the random-exploration condition. Repeat whole campaign three times. Measurement metrics: per-build wall-clock time, aggregated mean and median per sequence, speedup% = (clean_time - incremental_time)/clean_time, reproducibility rate measured as bitwise-equality of binaries (cmp), distribution of option-diff sizes between successive configurations, fraction of builds with negative speedup, number of uniquely rebuilt object files and rebuilt subsystems, and overall CPU-seconds consumed. Statistical tests: paired non-parametric test (Wilcoxon signed-rank) for time comparisons and bootstrap confidence intervals for speedup estimates. Ablation studies: (1) disable reproducibility deny list, (2) disable performance deny list, (3) vary mutation size {1,5,10,50} and record speedup and reproducibility, (4) vary number of bases n in {10,50,100,200} to test scalability, (5) compare PyroBuildS sequences to ordering-based incremental strategies on the same set of configurations when computationally feasible. Environment: repeat builds in isolated Docker containers on dedicated hardware with fixed CPU/core count and identical toolchains; report hardware and container specs. Record failed builds and exclude them only for reproducibility analysis but report failure rates per method. Risk Factors and Limitations: Solver and tooling scalability: dependency solver or kconfig-repair tools may fail or be too slow on very large configurations, producing an incomplete or biased set of variations. Non-deterministic build artifacts: toolchain-embedded timestamps, randomization, or host-specific metadata can produce unreproducible binaries unrelated to configuration differences. Deny-list quality dependence: the method relies on prior identification of problematic options; incomplete or incorrect deny lists can cause negative speedups or unreproducibility. Sampling bias: using randconfig or constrained samplers may not uniformly cover the configuration space; results may not generalize to other sampling strategies. Environment sensitivity: measured speedups depend on build system implementation (Make), language (C), and platform; results may not transfer to different build systems or languages. Computational cost: large-scale campaigns require substantial CPU-hours; experiments may be costly to reproduce. Generalization limits: approach is tailored to compile-time configuration variability and Make-like build workflows; it may not apply to runtime-only variability, interpreted languages, or non-Make build tools.
